title: Mastering LLM Inference Optimization From Theory to Cost Effective Deployment: Mark Moyou
talk_summary: NVIDIA architect explains LLM inference mechanics (prefill/decode, KV cache, batching) and how to measure production deployments via ISL/OSL distributions, TTFT, token latency, and completion time. Most concrete advice is for self-hosted GPU serving (TRT-LLM, FP8, in-flight batching), with limited direct applicability to API-only agent orchestration.

takeaways.technique: Measure ISL/OSL distribution before setting context budgets
takeaways.what_they_do: They build a 2D histogram of input sequence length vs output sequence length from production traffic, then size engines and max context/output to actual user patterns rather than provider maxima.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we use this to statistically determine what is the max input sequence length and the max output sequence length across all of my users

takeaways.technique: Route by measured query pattern, not one max config
takeaways.what_they_do: They test whether switching inference engine/config for a given query pattern still satisfies requests and how much cost/latency it saves, rather than using one max-sized configuration for all traffic.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if I switch the engine does it still satisfy the querying pattern and how much cost does it save

takeaways.what_they_do: In-flight batching injects a new request as soon as any request finishes instead of waiting for a batch barrier.
takeaways.evidence_quote: I don't have to wait for all the requests to finish to start a new request

takeaways.what_they_do: They track time-to-first-token, token-to-token latency, and total completion under real load to detect batching, scheduling, and memory-pressure drift.
takeaways.evidence_quote: time to First token so how long does it take me to generate
